::: {.callout-note}
## About this page

This page **tests the panzoom extension with the Jupyter engine**: the
same cell options as the R pages, on matplotlib figures. knitr and
Jupyter hand figures to Quarto differently (knitr writes the image
markdown itself; Jupyter cells come back as notebook outputs), so the
filter has to find the figures and their cell options either way. The
document has no `lightbox:` key, and only marked cells should open the
viewer.

Rendering it needs Python with matplotlib and ipykernel: see
[tests/README.md](https://github.com/sekoclancy/panzoom/blob/main/tests/README.md).

Jupyter leaves the `panzoom` and `lightbox` options out of the code shown
on the page (knitr shows them); the **Code** button at the top shows the
full source.

Headings carry what the browser test checks, as on the other pages:
`expect-open`, `expect-hint`, `expect-max-zoom`, `expect-fit` and
`expect-format` (`svg`: the viewer got a vector image).
:::

The cases below share this setup and helper:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def walk(ax, n=200, title=None):
    ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=n)))
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
```

## 1. `panzoom: true` {#c1 expect-open="panzoom" expect-hint="shown"}

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave."

x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```

## 2. Options overriding the defaults {#c2 expect-open="panzoom" expect-hint="hidden" expect-max-zoom="2"}

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   max-zoom: 2
#|   hint: false
#| fig-cap: "Zoom stops at 2, no hint."

plt.plot(x, np.cos(x))
plt.show()
```

## 3. Labeled figure with a description {#c3 expect-open="panzoom"}

@fig-scatter has a description with math and a cross-reference to
@fig-sub.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| panzoom:
#|   description: 'Points scattered around $y = x + \varepsilon$, with a "quote"; compare @fig-sub.'
#| fig-cap: "A scatter plot, $n = 100$."

pts = rng.normal(size=100)
plt.scatter(pts, pts + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=100))
plt.show()
```

## 4. Subfigures (fig-subcap, layout-ncol) {#c4 expect-open="panzoom"}

The two subfigures form a gallery.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sub
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "Two subfigures."
#| fig-subcap: ["A random walk", "A histogram"]
#| layout-ncol: 2

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
walk(ax)
plt.show()
plt.hist(rng.normal(size=500), bins=30)
plt.show()
```

## 5. Multi-plot cell with a group {#c5 expect-open="panzoom"}

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: walks
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "First walk."
#|   - "Second walk."

for i in range(2):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    walk(ax)
    plt.show()
```

## 6. Wide collage (8 × 0.8 in) {#c6 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height"}

A strip, so it opens at screen height. Jupyter figures are shown at their
size in inches × 96 px (Quarto writes it on the image), not shrunk to the
column as knitr's are: a 25 × 2 in collage would be 2,400 px wide on the
page, cut off at the column's edge. This one fits.

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "An 8 × 0.8 inch collage of 8 panels."

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(8, 0.8), layout="constrained")
for ax in axes:
    walk(ax)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
plt.show()
```

## 7. `panzoom: false` inside a `.panzoom` div {#c7 expect-open="nothing"}

::: {.panzoom}
```{python}
#| panzoom: false
#| fig-cap: "Left alone."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(2 * x))
plt.show()
```
:::

## 8. `classes: panzoom` {#c8 expect-open="panzoom"}

```{python}
#| classes: panzoom
#| fig-cap: "Marked with the classes cell option."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
```

## 9. Lightbox cell option only {#c9 expect-open="glightbox"}

Quarto's lightbox, not panzoom.

```{python}
#| lightbox: true
#| fig-cap: "Opened by Quarto's lightbox."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(4 * x))
plt.show()
```

## 10. Plain cell, no options {#c10 expect-open="nothing"}

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "No options: not opened."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(5 * x))
plt.show()
```

## 11. `panzoom` and `lightbox` options on one cell {#c11 expect-open="panzoom"}

Both options: panzoom wins, and the `lightbox:` options are dropped. (With
Jupyter, Quarto's lightbox ignores `#| lightbox:` with options under it
anyway, unlike with knitr; `lightbox: true` works, as in case 9.)

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "Both options: panzoom."
#| lightbox:
#|   group: both
#|   description: "Should not reach the lightbox."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(6 * x))
plt.show()
```

## 12. matplotlib as svg {#c12 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="contain" expect-format="svg"}

The same figure path as case 1, written as svg instead of png: Jupyter
saves the figure file itself, unlike knitr (svg from R is on
[E: image formats](e-formats.html)). The viewer redraws svg at each zoom,
so it stays sharp. Jupyter ignores a cell's `fig-format`, so the cell
switches matplotlib's output to svg itself, and back to png after.

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A damped wave, as svg."

%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["svg"]
plt.plot(x, np.exp(-x / 4) * np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["png"]
```
